name: Ryan F. Johnson, PhD
bio: Ryan F. Johnson is an associate professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University. His research focuses on predictive computational modeling of propulsion and reacting-flow systems, with interests spanning computational fluid dynamics, chemical kinetics, GPU-enabled high-performance computing, and embedded machine learning. He develops scalable prediction capabilities for complex, multiscale problems, with the goal of enabling accurate simulation of real propulsion and energy devices.

Before joining Carnegie Mellon, he was a scientist and aerospace engineer at the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington, DC, where he led efforts in high-speed propulsion modeling. He also held a visiting scholar appointment at Stanford University, where he worked on problems at the intersection of high-performance computing, CFD, and chemical kinetics.

Johnson received his Ph.D. from the University of Virginia in 2014 under the supervision of Professor Harsha Chelliah. He is a recipient of the Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE).
education: Ph.D. Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, UVA, 2014

name: George Tang
bio: George is a Ph.D. student in Mechanical Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, jointly advised by Professor Ryan Johnson and Professor Chris McComb. His research interests include connecting CFD and computational design together to better link and understand physical systems with mission-driven application.

George completed his undergraduate degree in Aerospace Engineering at the University of Maryland - College Park and his masters degree in Mechanical Engineering - Research at Carnegie Mellon University. He has worked on multiple engineering projects, which his masters research focused on wheel mobility for the NASA MoonRanger rover mission and also coursework projects ranging from automating FEA meshing workflows to topology optimization of a Formula 1 Racing Car piston through Laser Powder Bed Fusion during his time at CMU before PhD. He is also very motivated in mentoring and teaching students, where he served as a tutor for three courses and a TA for one course during his time at UMD and a Course Assistant for 24-261 2D mechanics during his time at CMU.
Outside of research and teaching, he enjoys going out to the bars around Pittsburgh, tailgating at football games, reading books, watching documentaries, and playing video games.
education: B.S. Aerospace Engineering, University of Maryland, College Park
M.S. Mechanical Engineering (Research), Carnegie Mellon University

name: Melik Demirel
bio: Melik is a Ph.D. student in Mechanical Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, jointly advised by Professors Francis Ogoke and Ryan Johnson. His research interests center on turbulence problems in additive manufacturing and propulsion systems using simulations and embedded machine learning methods.

Before joining CMU, he earned a B.S. in Aerospace Engineering from Penn State and worked as a Research and Development Engineer at the Penn State Applied Research Laboratory's CIMP-3D. His undergraduate research used computational fluid dynamics to study the effects of unsteady inlet turbulence on airfoil cascade performance, while his work at CIMP-3D focused on modeling and simulation for metal additive manufacturing. These experiences shaped his interest in computational approaches to turbulence across both fields.
Outside the lab, he enjoys producing electronic music and playing tennis.
education: B.S. Aerospace Engineering, Pennsylvania State University

name: Darren Kim
bio: Darren Kim is a Ph.D. student in Mechanical Engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, jointly advised by Professors Jessica Zhang and Ryan Johnson. His research interests focus on space- and combustion-related problems with applications in both commercial and government settings.

Before joining CMU, he earned a B.S. in Aerospace Engineering from the University of California, San Diego, with a specialization in Space and Astrodynamics. At UC San Diego, he conducted research in orbital and space mechanics involving multibody systems. He also worked on wing-reinforcement performance testing, machine-learning-based failure prediction, and a twin-axial drone configuration.
In addition to his research, Darren has written an educational textbook and created educational content.
Outside the lab, he enjoys fixating on difficult problems for hours on end. Good luck catching him sleeping.
education: B.S. Aerospace Engineering, University of California, San Diego
